claim: Cortical development in rhesus macaque recapitulates multiple facets of cortical development in humans, including the complex composition of neural stem cells and the thicker supragranular layer.
source: Cortical development in rhesus macaque is known to recapitulate multiple facets of cortical development in humans, including the complex composition of neural stem cells and the thicker supragranular layer.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about macaque and human cortical development.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing produced a transcriptomic atlas of developing parietal lobe in rhesus macaque neocortex from samples at E40, E50, E70, E80, and E90.
source: To characterize temporal shifts in transcriptomic programming responsible for differentiation from stem cells to neurons, we sampled parietal lobes of rhesus macaque at E40, E50, E70, E80, and E90, spanning the full period of prenatal neurogenesis. Single-cell RNA sequencing produced a transcriptomic atlas of developing parietal lobe in rhesus macaque neocortex.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach and data generation performed by the authors.

claim: Deep-layer neurons appear in the early stages of neurogenesis, while upper-layer neurons appear later.
source: Notably, deep-layer neurons appear in the early stages of neurogenesis, while upper-layer neurons appear later.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cell fates are determined post-mitotically in the macaque neocortex.
source: While these different lineages show overlap in their differentiation program, cell fates are determined post-mitotically.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by trajectory analysis data in the manuscript.

claim: Trajectories analysis from ventricular radial glia (vRGs) to outer radial glia (oRGs) revealed dynamic gene expression profiles and identified differential activation of BMP, FGF, and WNT signaling pathways between vRGs and oRGs.
source: Trajectories analysis from ventricular radial glia (vRGs) to outer radial glia (oRGs) revealed dynamic gene expression profiles and identified differential activation of BMP, FGF, and WNT signaling pathways between vRGs and oRGs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by trajectory analysis data in the manuscript.

claim: The dorsal neocortex can be anatomically divided into six layers of cells occupied by distinct neuronal cell types.
source: Generally, the dorsal neocortex can be anatomically divided into six layers of cells occupied by distinct neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about neocortex structure.

claim: Deep-layer neurons project to the thalamus (layer VI neurons) and subcortical areas (layer V neurons), while upper-layer neurons preferentially form intracortical projections.
source: The deep-layer neurons project to the thalamus (layer VI neurons) and subcortical areas (layer V neurons), while neurons occupying more superficial layers (upper-layer neurons) preferentially form intracortical projections (Jabaudon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jabaudon, 2017.

claim: The generation of distinct excitatory neuron cell types follows a temporal pattern in which early-born neurons migrate to deep layers (layers V and VI), while later-born neurons migrate and surpass early-born neurons to occupy the upper layers (layers II–IV).
source: The generation of distinct excitatory neuron (EN) cell types follows a temporal pattern in which early-born neurons migrate to deep layers (i.e. layers V and VI), while the later-born neurons migrate and surpass early-born neurons to occupy the upper layers (layers II–IV) (Rakic, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rakic, 1974.

claim: Daughter neurons exhibit the same transcriptional profiles of their respective progenitor radial glia, although these apparently heritable expression patterns fade as neurons mature.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), Telley and colleagues found that daughter neurons exhibit the same transcriptional profiles of their respective progenitor radial glia (RG), although these apparently heritable expression patterns fade as neurons mature (Telley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Telley et al., 2019.

claim: The neocortex of primates exhibits an extra neurogenesis zone known as the outer subventricular zone (OSVZ), which is not present in rodents.
source: The neocortex of primates exhibits an extra neurogenesis zone known as the outer subventricular zone (OSVZ), which is not present in rodents.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences between primate and rodent neocortex development.

claim: Outer radial glia (oRG) cells retain basal processes but lack apical junctions.
source: Although ventricular radial glia (vRG) is also found in humans and NHP, the vast majority of RG in these higher species occupy the OSVZ and are therefore termed outer radial glia (oRG). oRG cells retain basal processes but lack apical junctions (Hansen et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2010.

claim: oRG cells divide in a process known as mitotic somal translocation, which differs from vRG.
source: oRG cells retain basal processes but lack apical junctions (Hansen et al., 2010) and divide in a process known as mitotic somal translocation, which differs from vRG (Ostrem et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ostrem et al., 2014.

claim: vRG and oRG are both accompanied by the expression of stem cell markers such as PAX6 and exhibit extensive self-renewal and proliferative capacities.
source: vRG and oRG are both accompanied by the expression of stem cell markers such as PAX6 and exhibit extensive self-renewal and proliferative capacities (Betizeau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Betizeau et al., 2013.

claim: HOPX is a molecular marker for oRGs, while CRYAB and FBXO32 are markers for vRGs.
source: Previous scRNA-seq analyses have identified several molecular markers, including HOPX for oRGs, CRYAB, and FBXO32 for vRGs (Pollen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pollen et al., 2015.

claim: oRGs are derived from vRGs.
source: Furthermore, oRGs are derived from vRGs, and vRGs exhibit obvious differences in numerous cell-extrinsic mechanisms, including activation of the FGF-MAPK cascade, SHH, PTEN/AKT, and PDGF pathways, and oxygen (O2) levels.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Rhesus macaque and humans share multiple aspects of neurogenesis.
source: Rhesus macaque and humans share multiple aspects of neurogenesis, and more importantly, the rhesus monkey and human brains share more similar gene expression patterns than the brains of mice and humans (Bakken et al., 2016; Bernard et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bakken et al., 2016; Bernard et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2012.

claim: A total of 53,259 cells remained after quality control for subsequent analysis.
source: We obtained a transcriptomic atlas from 53,259 cells after filtering out low-quality cells and removing potential doublets.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing results.

claim: 28 distinct cell clusters were identified using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of dimension reduction using Seurat.
source: Each embedding was visualized using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of dimension reduction using Seurat, which identified 28 distinct cell clusters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the clustering analysis results.

claim: vRG (cluster 10) showed characteristic VIM and PAX6 expression.
source: In general, vRG (cluster 10) showed characteristic VIM and PAX6 expression
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: oRG (cluster 12 and cluster 14) highly expressed HOPX.
source: oRG (cluster 12 and cluster 14) highly expressed HOPX, previously verified marker (Pollen et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and a citation to Pollen et al., 2015.

claim: Two clusters of IPCs (cluster 8 and cluster 22) strongly expressed EOMES.
source: two clusters (cluster 8 and cluster 22) of IPCs that strongly expressed EOMES
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ENs were identified by the expression of well-established markers, such as NEUROD2 and NEUROD6.
source: ENs were identified by the expression of well-established markers, such as NEUROD2 and NEUROD6
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and established knowledge of neuronal markers.

claim: The astrocyte and oligodendrocyte lineages were identified by AQP4 and SOX10 expression, respectively.
source: and the astrocyte and oligodendrocyte lineages were identified by AQP4 and SOX10 expression, respectively (Silbereis et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and a citation to Silbereis et al., 2010.

claim: Cortical neural progenitors undergo neurogenesis processes during the early stages of macaque prenatal cortical development, while gliogenic differentiation, including oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, occurs in later stages.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that cortical neural progenitors undergo neurogenesis processes during the early stages of macaque prenatal cortical development, while gliogenic differentiation, including oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, occurs in later stages (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 1A and B.

claim: All EN subclusters could be distinguished by differential expression of either deep-layer neuron markers (BCL11B, FEZF2, and SOX5) or upper-layer neuron markers (CUX1 and SATB2).
source: We found that all EN subclusters could be well distinguished by differential expression of either deep-layer neuron markers (BCL11B, FEZF2, and SOX5) (Tsyporin et al., 2021) or upper-layer neuron markers (CUX1 and SATB2) (Li et al., 2020; He et al., 2017; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data, citations to Tsyporin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; He et al., 2017, and Figure 2B and C.

claim: Early-born neurons (E40 and E50) predominantly outnumbered later-born neurons in the deep-layer neuron subclusters (EN5 and E10), while upper-layer neuron subclusters contained the inverse proportions.
source: In agreement with this early work, we found that early-born neurons (E40 and E50) predominantly outnumbered later-born neurons in the deep-layer neuron subclusters (EN5 and E10), while upper-layer neuron subclusters contained the inverse proportions (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and Figure 2C and D.

claim: EN5 and EN10 (deep-layer neurons) subclusters emerged at E40 and E50 and disappeared in later stages.
source: While the EN5 and EN10 (deep-layer neurons) subclusters emerged at E40 and E50 and disappeared in later stages
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of cell populations.

claim: EN subclusters 1, 2, 3, and 4 gradually increased in population size from E50 to E80.
source: EN subclusters 1, 2, 3, and 4 gradually increased in population size from E50 to E80
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of cell populations.

claim: EN subclusters 8 and 9 gradually increased in population size from E80 to E90.
source: EN subclusters 8 and 9 gradually increased in population size from E80 to E90 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of cell populations and Figure 2D.

claim: EN6 was exclusively found in the cortex at E70.
source: Notably, EN6 was exclusively found in the cortex at E70 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A set of genes previously reported as highly expressed in oRG showed high expression in the oRG_C12 differentiated pseudotime terminal, including SFRP1, HOPX, FAM107A, TNC, PTN, and MOXD1.
source: We found a set of genes that were previously reported as highly expressed in ORG that also showed high expression in the oRG_C12 differentiated pseudotime terminal (Pollen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2018) (such as SFRP1, HOPX, FAM107A, TNC, PTN, and MOXD1)
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis data and citations to Pollen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2018.

claim: High ASPM expression was typical of cells in the earlier, RG, pseudotime terminal.
source: while high ASPM expression was typical of cells in the earlier, RG, pseudotime terminal (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis data and Figure 3F.

claim: RGCC, which controls mitotic spindle orientation, was enriched at the oRG_C12 terminal.
source: In addition to these markers, we also found enrichment for some potential regulatory genes at the oRG_C12 terminal, such as regulator of the cell cycle (RGCC), which controls mitotic spindle orientation (Guo et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and a citation to Guo et al., 2021.

claim: TTYH1, which regulates cell adhesion, was enriched at the oRG_C12 terminal.
source: and TTYH1, which regulates cell adhesion (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and a citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: Genes that regulate excitability and ionic gradients in neurons, such as ATP1A2, ATP1B2, and SCN4B, were found at the oRG terminal and were not previously known to participate in oRG differentiation.
source: We also found genes that regulate excitability and ionic gradients in neurons, such as ATP1A2, ATP1B2, and SCN4B, which were not previously known to participate in oRG differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and represents a novel finding.

claim: Cell cycle-related genes such as MKI67, TOP2A, CDC20, and CCNA2 were identified as DEGs specific to the RG pseudotime terminal.
source: Analysis of DEGs specific to the RG pseudotime terminal identified cell cycle-related genes such as MKI67, TOP2A, CDC20, and CCNA2.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Glial-specific genes such as SLC1A3, ZFP36L1, GFAP, DBI, and EDNRB exhibited high expression in the oRG_C12 terminal.
source: Within the glia-like cells that largely comprised the oRG_C12 terminal, we also detected a population of glial-specific genes that exhibited high expression such as SLC1A3, ZFP36L1 (Weng et al., 2019), GFAP, DBI, and EDNRB (Gadea et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to Weng et al., 2019 and Gadea et al., 2008.

claim: Several DEGs that have not yet been investigated in RG function and differentiation were uncovered, such as DKK3, DDAH1, SAT1, and PEA15.
source: In addition, our analyses uncovered several DEGs that have not yet been investigated in RG function and differentiation, such as DKK3, DDAH1, SAT1, and PEA15.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and represents novel findings.

claim: Mapping genes, such as FEZF2 and DOK5, may play a role in RG cells to specify neuronal progeny.
source: We hypothesized that mapping genes, such as FEZF2 and DOK5, may play a role in RG cells to specify neuronal progeny (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the analysis of overlapping genes between RG and neurons, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Apical progenitors and daughter ENs share molecular temporal identities during neocortex prenatal corticogenesis.
source: Our results provide single-cell transcriptome data to support that apical progenitors and daughter ENs share molecular temporal identities during neocortex prenatal corticogenesis (; Lin et al., 2021; Shu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and citations to Lin et al., 2021; Shu et al., 2019.

claim: A bifurcating trajectory from neural stem cells leads to either deep-layer neurons in one branch or to upper-layer neurons in the alternative branch.
source: Using Dynverse R packages, we constructed pseudotime trajectories for the cluster data, which identified a bifurcating trajectory from neural stem cells (including RG_C10, oRG_C12, and oRG_C14) that leads to either deep-layer neurons in one branch or to upper-layer neurons in the alternative branch (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis and Figure 4C.

claim: The two distinct neuronal fates share a common path from neural stem cells to immature neurons, supporting the likelihood that neuronal fate is primarily determined post-mitotically.
source: However, it should be noted that the two distinct fates share a common path from neural stem cells to immature neurons (Figure 4C, from dot 1 to dot 4), supporting the likelihood that neuronal fate is primarily determined post-mitotically.
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis and Figure 4C, and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Most DEGs, such as STMN2, TUBB3, NEUROD2, and NEUROD6, were shared between both deep-layer and upper-layer branches, illustrating the common differentiation processes between deep- and upper-layer ENs.
source: More specifically, we found that most DEGs, such as STMN2, TUBB3, NEUROD2, and NEUROD6, were shared between both branches, illustrating the common differentiation processes between deep- and upper-layer ENs.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis along trajectories.

claim: Deep-layer-specific DEGs include FEZF2, TBR1, and LMO3.
source: We also identified deep-layer-specific DEGs (including FEZF2, TBR1, and LMO3)
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Upper-layer-specific genes include MEF2C and DOK5.
source: and upper-layer-specific genes (including MEF2C and DOK5).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: All major cell types were well integrated between human, macaque, and mouse species in the LIGER integration analysis.
source: Species-integrated UMAP showed that all major cell types were well integrated between the three species (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cross-species integration analysis and Figure 5A.

claim: Similar cellular processes with comparable temporal progression sequentially generate deep-layer and upper-layer neurons in both primates and rodents.
source: It is clearly observed that similar cellular processes with comparable temporal progression sequentially generate deep-layer and upper-layer neurons in both primates and rodents (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A to C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-species comparison and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A to C.

claim: In primates, the number and relative development period of upper neurons are more extended than that of rodents.
source: However, in primates, the number and relative development period of upper neurons are more extended than that of rodents (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-species comparison and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Strong expression of the oRG marker genes, such as HOPX, MOXD1, FAM107A, and CLU, was found in both human and macaque datasets, while barely detectable expression was found in mouse dataset.
source: Our cross-species analysis showed strong expression of the oRG marker genes, such as HOPX, MOXD1, FAM107A, and CLU in both human and macaque datasets (Figure 5B), while barely detectable expression in mouse dataset, which is consistent with previous reports (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-species gene expression analysis, Figure 5B, and a citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: The biological process of vRG-to-IPC is remarkably conserved across human, macaque, and mouse species.
source: Comparing vRG-to-IPC trajectory between human, macaque, and mouse, we found this biological process of vRG-to-IPC is remarkably conserved across species.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-species trajectory analysis.

claim: The vRG-to-oRG trajectory is divergent between species because the oRG population was not identified in the mouse dataset.
source: However, the vRG-to-oRG trajectory is divergent between species because the oRG population was not identified in the mouse dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-species trajectory analysis.

claim: A total of 72 homologous TFs were shared between human, macaque, and mouse transcriptomes.
source: A total of 72 homologous TFs were shared between human, macaque, and mouse transcriptomes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the comparative analysis results.

claim: The majority of TFs had conserved temporal dynamics between species, indicating evolutionarily conserved patterns of regulation in neural stem cell differentiation.
source: Analysis of their temporal dynamics revealed that they exhibited similar temporal patterns between species such as NEUROD1, NEUROG2, POU3F2, ETV1, ETV5, and FOS (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which indicated that the majority of TFs had conserved temporal dynamics between species, and thus evolutionarily conserved patterns of regulation in neural stem cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal expression analysis, Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Classical developmental TFs such as GATA1, SOX2, HMGN3, TCF7L1, ZFX, EMX2, SOX10, NEUROG1, NEUROD1, and POU3F1 show commonalities in regulatory activity across human, macaque, and mouse prenatal neocortical neurogenesis.
source: Analysis of the regulatory activity of human, macaque, and mouse (Di Bella et al., 2021) prenatal neocortical neurogenesis indicated commonalities in the roles of classical developmental TFs such as GATA1, SOX2, HMGN3, TCF7L1, ZFX, EMX2, SOX10, NEUROG1, NEUROD1, and POU3F1.
evidence: This claim is supported by SCENIC regulatory network analysis and a citation to Di Bella et al., 2021.

claim: Some conserved regulatory TFs present in more than one species include HMGN3, EMX2, SOX2, and HMGA2 at the deep-layer generation stage and SOX10, ZNF672, and ZNF672 at the upper-layer generation stage.
source: Some conserved regulatory TFs present in more than one species are identified, such as HMGN3, EMX2, SOX2, and HMGA2, at the deep-layer generation stage and SOX10, ZNF672, and ZNF672 at the upper-layer generation stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-species regulatory network analysis.

claim: The parietal lobe is the center of the somatic senses and is significant for interpreting words as well as language understanding and processing.
source: The parietal lobe is the center of the somatic senses and is significant for interpreting words as well as language understanding and processing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about parietal lobe function.

claim: The existence of oRGs has long been demonstrated in humans and primates through live imaging and immunostaining.
source: The existence of oRGs has long been demonstrated in humans and primates through live imaging and immunostaining (Hansen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2010.

claim: oRGs share similarities in their patterns of gene expression with vRGs (e.g. SOX2, PAX6, and NESTIN) but also specifically express several genes (such as MOXD1, HOPX, and FAM107A).
source: ORGs share similarities in their patterns of gene expression with vRGs (e.g. SOX2, PAX6, and NESTIN) but also specifically express several genes (such as MOXD1, HOPX, and FAM107A) (Pollen et al., 2015; Nowakowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pollen et al., 2015; Nowakowski et al., 2016.

claim: Hyperpolarization in mouse apical progenitors has been shown to promote the generation of IPCs and indirect neurogenesis.
source: Indeed, hyperpolarization in mouse apical progenitors has been shown to promote the generation of IPCs and indirect neurogenesis (Vitali et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vitali et al., 2018.

claim: FEZF2 and SOX5 have been confirmed to be associated with deep-layer neuron specification in mice.
source: Notably, FEZF2 (Molyneaux et al., 2005) and SOX5 Leone et al., 2008 have been confirmed associated with deep-layer neuron specification in mice
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molyneaux et al., 2005 and Leone et al., 2008.

claim: TMOD1, PID1, and LINGO1 have not been reported before in the context of cortical projection neuron fate specification.
source: while others, such as TMOD1, PID1, and LINGO1, have not been reported before, and their potential functions in the fate specification of cortical projection neurons need to be further explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of findings and a suggestion for future research.

claim: Extending neurogenesis by transplanting mouse embryos to a rat mother increases explicitly the number of upper-layer cortical neurons, with concomitant abundant neurogenic progenitors in the sub-VZ.
source: Previous study evidence had shown that extending neurogenesis by transplanting mouse embryos to a rat mother increases explicitly the number of upper-layer cortical neurons, with concomitant abundant neurogenic progenitors in the sub-VZ (Stepien et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stepien et al., 2020.

claim: The BD Rhapsody microwells might be less efficient in capturing mature ENs but have a good capture effect on newborn neurons at each sampling time point.
source: Due to the fixed size of the BD Rhapsody microwells, this sing-cell capture method might be less efficient in capturing mature ENs but has a good capture effect on newborn neurons at each sampling time point.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of the method used.

claim: Timed pregnancy-derived biological replicate specimens were profiled at each prenatal developmental stage (E40, E50, E70, E80, and E90).
source: Timed pregnancy-derived biological replicate specimens were profiled at each prenatal developmental stage (E40, E50, E70, E80, and E90) (Bakken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with a citation to Bakken et al., 2016.

claim: These time points were selected to coincide with peak periods of neurogenesis for the different layers of the neocortex based on previous studies.
source: These time points were selected to coincide with peak periods of neurogenesis for the different layers of the neocortex based on previous studies (Bakken et al., 2016 ; Lein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bakken et al., 2016 and Lein et al., 2017.

claim: All animal procedures followed international standards and were approved in advance by the Ethics Committee on Laboratory Animals at IMBCAMS.
source: All animal procedures followed international standards and were approved in advance by the Ethics Committee on Laboratory Animals at IMBCAMS (Institute of Medical Biology, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Eight pregnancy-derived fetal brains of rhesus macaque (M. mulatta) were collected at five prenatal developmental stages (E40, E50, E70, E80, E90).
source: We collected eight pregnancy-derived fetal brains of rhesus macaque (M. mulatta) at five prenatal developmental stages (E40, E50, E70, E80, E90) and dissected the parietal lobe cortex.
evidence: This is a description of the sample collection.

claim: Single-cell capture was achieved by random distribution of a single-cell suspension across >200,000 microwells through a limited dilution approach.
source: Single-cell capture was achieved by random distribution of a single-cell suspension across >200,000 microwells through a limited dilution approach.
evidence: This is a description of the technical method used.

claim: Cells were filtered to retain only higher quality (with less than 7.5% mitochondrial gene counts, less than 5.5% ribosomal gene counts, and detected genes above 400 and less than 6000).
source: Then, cells were filtered to retain only higher quality (with less than 7.5% mitochondrial gene counts, less than 5.5% ribosomal gene counts, and detected genes above 400 and less than 6000).
evidence: This is a description of the quality control criteria applied.

claim: Cell doublets were identified using Scrublet v0.142 with default parameters and removed before data analysis.
source: Additionally, we identified cell doublets using Scrublet v0.142 with default parameters and removed doublets before data analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the quality control method used.
